title: Pre-Purchase Ship Inspection Rotterdam | Lay-By & Terminals
description: Pre-purchase inspection in Rotterdam for buyers of tankers, bulk carriers and container ships: tanks, holds, deck and machinery checked at lay-bys or terminals.
h1: Inspecting a second-hand ship for a buyer at Rotterdam, from the Botlek jetties to Maasvlakte
intro: Rotterdam is where many voyages end, and a ship that has just discharged is often the easiest one for a buyer to see properly. Tankers finishing at Europoort, chemical tankers moving between Botlek and Pernis jetties, Capesizes emptied at Maasvlakte and ships idle on lay-by berths all offer inspection windows of different lengths. Our pre-purchase inspection in Rotterdam measures as well as looks: spot thickness readings, crack checks, hatch cover and deck machinery checks and machinery readings, reported to the buyer while the window is open. The technicians fly from India for each job, holding Schengen visas obtained for it.

highlights.h: Lay-by berths give the longest look
highlights.p: A ship idle on a lay-by berth or buoy between cargoes is the best Rotterdam setting for a buyer. Ballast tanks can be emptied and ventilated, safe access rigged and machinery run, with no cargo operation competing for the crew's time or closing parts of the deck.

highlights.h: Discharge windows for bulkers and tankers
highlights.p: After an ore or coal discharge at Maasvlakte, a bulk carrier's holds are empty and dry for a short spell before she ballasts out. A crude tanker at Europoort offers deck, accommodation and engine room under the terminal's permit while her cargo goes ashore.

highlights.h: Schengen visas set the first date
highlights.p: Every technician travelling from India needs a Schengen visa, and that lead time, not the flight, decides how soon we can board. Buyers who expect a Rotterdam viewing should tell us when the ship is first fixed to call, even before the date is firm.

sections.h: Where in Rotterdam can a buyer inspect a ship?
p: Each district suits a different kind of inspection. At the crude and product terminals of Europoort and Maasvlakte, the terminal's safety rules allow work on deck, in the accommodation and in the engine room during discharge under a permit, while tank entry waits. The chemical and product jetties at Botlek and Pernis see parcel tankers shift berth several times in one call, so an inspection there is planned around each move, with the pump-room and cargo-piping work fitted into the hours between parcels. At the Maasvlakte container and bulk terminals, the cargo plan sets the window.

The lay-by berths and buoys inside the port are where a buyer gets the fullest picture of a trading ship, because nothing competes with the inspection for the crew's attention. The anchorages off the Maasmond allow a launch boarding when the ship cannot come in, at the expense of what can be opened safely at sea. A ship in one of Damen Shiprepair's Botlek docks shows her bottom and side shell dry, but a visit needs the yard's agreement as well as the seller's.
list: Lay-by berths and buoys: the fullest scope on a trading ship, with ballast tanks and holds prepared
Europoort and Maasvlakte oil terminals: deck, accommodation and engine room during discharge, under permit
Botlek and Pernis jetties: chemical and product tankers between parcels, for pump room and cargo piping
Maasvlakte bulk and container terminals: holds after discharge, hatch covers, deck and scrubber piping
Anchorages off the Maasmond: launch boarding, limited to spaces that can be made safe at anchor
Botlek repair docks: dry hull, propeller, rudder and sea chests, with the yard's agreement

sections.h: Which ships are bought and inspected in Rotterdam?
p: Product and chemical tankers are the most frequent subjects, because North West Europe's refining and chemical trades keep a large fleet of them moving through Botlek, Pernis and Europoort, and European owners sell older units on as they renew their fleets. Crude tankers discharging at Europoort, Capesize and Panamax bulk carriers emptied of ore and coal at Maasvlakte, feeders and short-sea ships, LPG carriers and the ro-ro ships serving the UK and Ireland complete the picture.

What the buyer needs to know depends on where the ship is going next. Some buyers plan to move older tonnage into trades outside Europe; others want to keep a ship on European routes, where emissions trading and FuelEU Maritime now weigh on every voyage, and need to know whether she can stand another five-year cycle. Either way the question is the same: what will the next renewal survey and docking ask of her in steel, coatings and machinery, and what does the evidence on board say about it?

sections.h: How is a Rotterdam pre-purchase inspection scoped for a tanker or bulk carrier?
p: On a product or chemical tanker the plan starts from what the cargo programme allows. Cargo tanks being cleaned on a lay-by berth may be certified for entry, and the buyer then sees coatings or stainless steel directly; at a jetty they stay closed. Double-hull ballast spaces, the pump room or the cargo pump stacks on ships with deepwell pumps, cargo and heating lines on deck, manifold supports and vapour return piping are inspected wherever access allows. On a ship with an exhaust gas cleaning system, the wash-water and overboard lines and the shell around the discharge get spot thickness readings, because a scrubber in poor condition is a heavy inheritance for a buyer who will trade inside the North Sea emission control area.

On a bulk carrier freshly emptied at Maasvlakte, the inspection goes into the holds before the crew washes them or the ship ballasts: lower frames and brackets, hopper plating, tank tops and transverse bulkheads, with readings at several heights on the frames. Topside tanks follow if the master can release them. Weather counts on deck. North Sea winters bring rain and wind that slow deck work and spoil thermal images taken outdoors, so external surveys are planned for the drier part of the day and indoor machinery readings fill the rest.

sections.h: What do buyers usually learn from an inspection in Rotterdam?
p: Findings depend on the trade, but certain patterns come up again and again on the ships offered for sale here, and each is reported with its location, readings and photographs so the buyer and the broker can judge it against the class records.
list: Cargo tank coating damage on chemical tankers from aggressive parcels and repeated tank cleaning
Wastage and pitting on tanker deck plating and in double-bottom ballast spaces
Lower frame, bracket and hopper wastage in bulk carrier holds after years of ore and coal
Wall loss in scrubber wash-water and overboard piping, and corrosion around the shell outlet
Cracking at hatch corners and coaming brackets on container ships and bulk carriers
Corroded heating coils and deck lines on product and chemical tankers
Machinery running out of balance or with bearing wear, and switchboard hot spots under load

sections.h: How should a buyer plan a pre-purchase inspection at Rotterdam?
p: The visa is the first item. Each technician travelling from India applies for a Schengen visa for the job, so tell us as soon as Rotterdam appears on the ship's itinerary or in the sale discussions, and we plan the mobilisation around it. The team arrives through Amsterdam Schiphol and reaches the port by train and road. The seller's agent registers the technicians for ISPS access to the terminal or berth, or books a launch for an anchorage boarding.

If the buyer has any choice, ask the seller whether the ship can be seen on a lay-by berth after discharge rather than at the terminal during it. The difference in what can be opened, entered and run is large, and the report then covers more of the ship and leaves fewer items for the buyer to weigh without evidence. The ship's port state control inspections under the Paris MoU, published on Equasis, are worth reading before the visit, and anything they raise can be added to the inspection plan.

sections.h: Example scope: a chemical tanker between parcels at Botlek
p: A buyer interested in a coated chemical tanker trading parcels out of Botlek and Pernis may get only the hours between jetties. A practical plan starts in the double-hull ballast spaces the crew has prepared, reading bottom, side and stringer plating and rating coatings, then moves to the deck: cargo and heating lines, the manifold area, vent risers and the pump stacks, with deck plating read on a grid over the cargo block.

A cargo tank is entered only if it has been cleaned and certified for the next parcel and the seller agrees, in which case its coating is examined for blistering, breakdown and repaired areas. In the engine room, generators and the hydraulic power pack driving the cargo pumps are measured running, and the switchboards are surveyed under load. Records complete the visit: the cargo record book and tank cleaning history, the coating inspection records and the Certificate of Fitness for the chemicals she carries. The report sorts each finding by whether it touches class, the next charterer's vetting or only the new owner's maintenance plan.

codes: Norwegian Saleform 2012 and SALEFORM 2025 – the buyers' inspection
IACS UR Z10.3 (chemical tankers) and Z10.4 (double-hull oil tankers) – enhanced surveys
IACS UR Z7 – hull classification surveys and coating condition ratings
IBC Code – carriage of dangerous chemicals in bulk and the Certificate of Fitness
ASTM E797 – manual pulse-echo ultrasonic thickness measurement
deliverables: Summary of decision-relevant findings sent to the buyer before the team leaves the berth
Condition of tanks, holds, deck and pump room by space, with coating ratings and located photographs
Spot thickness readings, including scrubber wash-water and overboard piping where fitted
Crack-check results at hatch corners, brackets and other fatigue details
Vibration and thermal readings on running machinery, with the load at the time
Record review notes and a list of items not inspected, with reasons

faqs.q: Can a ship be inspected for a buyer during discharge at a Rotterdam terminal?
faqs.a: Partly. Terminal safety rules allow deck, accommodation and engine room work under a permit while cargo is worked, but cargo tanks stay closed and the crew is busy. On a bulk carrier, the holds become available as each one is emptied. If the ship moves to a lay-by berth afterwards, ask the seller whether the inspection can be held there instead, where ballast tanks can be prepared and more machinery run.

faqs.q: How soon can an inspection team reach Rotterdam from India?
faqs.a: The Schengen visa sets the pace. Each technician applies for one for the job, so the earliest boarding date depends on when we hear about the viewing. Tell us as soon as the ship is expected at Rotterdam, even with an approximate date, and send her name, location and the buyer's priorities to info@atlantisndt.com. The team then flies into Schiphol and travels on to the port.

faqs.q: Do you inspect the scrubber on a ship being sold at Rotterdam?
faqs.a: Yes, as part of the hull and machinery scope. We read wall thickness on the scrubber's wash-water inlet and outlet pipes, on the overboard line and on the shell plating around the discharge, where acidic water causes the fastest loss, and note the condition of the scrubber casing where it can be seen. Whether the system may be run in port depends on the current local rules, which the agent should confirm.

faqs.q: Is a pre-purchase inspection at Rotterdam accepted by the classification society?
faqs.a: Not for class credit. That needs readings taken by a thickness measurement firm the ship's classification society recognises under IACS UR Z17, and Atlantis has not yet completed that process with DNV, Lloyd's Register or ABS. A pre-purchase inspection is not a class survey and does not need class credit. Its readings inform the buyer's decision alongside the class records the society releases with the seller's consent.

faqs.q: Can the buyer see the ship's bottom before purchase in Rotterdam?
faqs.a: Only if she is in dock. At a berth, buoy or anchorage the shell below the waterline cannot be seen, so the buyer relies on the last dry-docking report, the hull survey records and any thickness report for it. If the ship is booked into a Botlek dock around the viewing window, ask the seller whether the inspection can be held there; with the yard's agreement, the buyer then sees the bottom, propeller, rudder and sea chests directly.

faqs.q: Can you inspect a ship in Rotterdam if the buyer's superintendent cannot travel?
faqs.a: Yes. Many buyers rely on the report alone. We agree the plan with the buyer or the broker before boarding, contact the buyer's technical department during the visit when a finding needs a decision on scope, and send the summary before the team leaves the ship. Photographs are tied to their positions on the general arrangement, so the buyer can see exactly where each finding sits.
